PullRequest.Title: Git - sign merge commits when git.enableCommitSigning is enabled
PullRequest.Body:

Fixes #116913

## Repro steps

1. In a repository, configure commit signing (for example SSH signing: `gpg.format=ssh`, `user.signingkey=<tmp>/key.pub`) and make sure git's own `commit.gpgSign` is not enabled.
2. Set `"git.enableCommitSigning": true`.
3. Have two diverging branches (`main` and `feature`), with `main` checked out.
4. Run **Git: Merge...** and pick `feature`. Merging a branch from the Repositories view or the Source Control Graph behaves the same way.
5. Run `git log --format='%h %G? %s' -1`.

**Expected:** the merge commit is signed (`G`). **Actual:** it is unsigned (`N`), even though regular commits made from VS Code with the same setting are signed.

## Root cause

`git.enableCommitSigning` is only applied in the commit flow: `CommandCenter.smartCommit` sets `opts.signCommit = true`, and `Repository.commit()` in `git.ts` passes `-S`. `Repository.merge()` in `git.ts` always ran a plain `git merge <ref>`, so a clean merge, which creates its merge commit inside `git merge`, ignored the setting.

A conflicted merge is already signed: after you resolve the conflicts, it's concluded through the regular commit flow, which passes `-S`.

## Fix

- `Repository.merge()` in `repository.ts` reads `git.enableCommitSigning`, scoped to the repository root, and passes `{ signCommit }` down. This mirrors how commit reads the setting.
- `Repository.merge()` in `git.ts` adds `-S` only when `signCommit` is `true`.
- When the setting is `false` or unset, the command line is unchanged (`git merge <ref>`), so git's own `commit.gpgSign` / `merge.gpgSign` configuration keeps applying. No `--no-gpg-sign` is ever passed.
- `-S` is harmless for fast-forward merges, since no commit is created.

All merge entry points (the **Git: Merge...** command, merging from the Repositories view or Graph, and the `Repository.merge` extension API) go through `Repository.merge()`, so all of them pick up the fix.

### Related operations with the same gap (not changed here)

Other commit-creating operations that VS Code runs also don't honour `git.enableCommitSigning`; they rely only on git's own config. Only `merge` is fixed here, to keep this change narrow and matched to the issue:

- `cherryPick` (`git cherry-pick <hash>`): commands and Graph cherry-pick.
- `rebase` (`git rebase`, also via the API) and `rebaseContinue` (`git rebase --continue`, used when committing during a rebase).
- `pull` when it creates a merge commit (`git pull`).

`cherry-pick` and `rebase` accept `-S`, so they could be follow-ups.

## Validation

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `pnpm run gulp compile-extension:git` | Passed (0 errors) |
| `node_modules/.bin/tsc -p extensions/git/tsconfig.json --noEmit` | Passed |
| `pnpm run oxlint extensions/git/src/git.ts extensions/git/src/repository.ts` | Passed (no findings) |
| `./scripts/test-integration.sh --suite git` | Passed: 91 passing, 2 pending, 0 failing |
| Pre-commit hygiene hook (oxlint + hygiene on the 2 changed files) | Passed |
| CLI check in a scratch repo with SSH signing and `commit.gpgsign=false`: `git merge feature` vs `git merge -S feature` | `N Merge branch 'feature'` vs `G Merge branch 'feature'`; fast-forward with `-S` succeeds |
| UI scenario (`validate-ui-scenario`, Code OSS dev build, throwaway profile) | Before: fails at "merge commit has a good signature" (`%G? = N`). After: all 4 steps pass (`%G? = G`) |

No unit test was added: the change doesn't add or extract a pure function. Existing integration tests cover the `merge` code path when the setting is unset, so the arguments are unchanged.

## Evidence

The UI scenario ran on a Code OSS dev build (macOS arm64, `Dev` quality) with a throwaway profile. It uses a scratch repository under `<tmp>` with a throwaway, passphrase-less SSH signing key configured only in the repository's local git config (`gpg.format=ssh`, `user.signingkey`, `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile`, `commit.gpgsign=false`). The scratch repo's `.vscode/settings.json` seeds `"git.enableCommitSigning": true`. The scenario:

1. opens the repository and the `.vscode/settings.json` file;
2. runs **Git: Merge...** and picks `feature`;
3. runs `git --no-pager log --format='%h %G? %s' -4; echo; git --no-pager log --show-signature -1` in the integrated terminal;
4. asserts `git log -1 --format=%G?` is `G`.

The same scenario was recorded with the fix reverted (before) and with the fix applied (after). A side-by-side video (before on the left, after on the right, aligned by step) and before/after screenshots of the terminal output are available on request. `gh` can't attach them to the PR. They show the same flow; the only difference is the signature status of the merge commit.

**Before (without fix):** terminal output

```
$ git --no-pager log --format='%h %G? %s' -4; echo; git --no-pager log --show-signature -1
d2f4cd3 N Merge branch 'feature'
650708d N Update main
eb0b4bd N Add feature
a5d86e8 N Initial commit

commit d2f4cd3c5c0b1c9ee1fdbbd28c83906ac321cc50 (HEAD -> main)
Merge: 650708d eb0b4bd
Author: Demo <demo@example.com>

    Merge branch 'feature'
```

Scenario result: `FAIL MS-04 Verify the merge commit has a good signature (%G? = G): Merge commit d2f4cd3 is not signed: %G? = N.`

**After (with fix):** terminal output

```
$ git --no-pager log --format='%h %G? %s' -4; echo; git --no-pager log --show-signature -1
bdd8a5e G Merge branch 'feature'
2649b8c N Update main
3e1904b N Add feature
b56c91c N Initial commit

commit bdd8a5e73bae7f0179eb4660dc86bb933d09cee3 (HEAD -> main)
Good "git" signature for demo@example.com with ED25519 key SHA256:...
Merge: 2649b8c 3e1904b
Author: Demo <demo@example.com>

    Merge branch 'feature'
```

Scenario result: `PASS MS-04 Verify the merge commit has a good signature (%G? = G): Merge commit bdd8a5e has a good signature: %G? = G (demo@example.com).`

The setup commits stay `N` in both runs because they were created with `commit.gpgsign=false` outside VS Code. Only the merge commit created by VS Code changes from `N` to `G`.

Scenarios.Scenario: Merge from the command palette, Repositories view, Graph, or extension API with git.enableCommitSigning disabled or unset
Scenarios.CriticalPath: A synchronous in-process configuration lookup completes before the existing repository operation starts; then the existing `git merge <ref>` subprocess and existing post-operation model refresh must finish before the merge promise resolves.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One per merge invocation, with only the pre-existing sequential repository-lock retry behavior.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same single subprocess ran with the same arguments when signing was disabled or unset.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Creates or advances the merge and must complete before model refresh and command completion.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Refresh HEAD, remotes, submodules, worktrees, operation markers, status, and refs after the mutating operation; several reads are parallelized and status/refs may invoke Git.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One bounded refresh per merge result, independent of branch or changed-file count except for the data returned by status/refs.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The identical post-merge refresh already followed every merge.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The existing refresh is awaited before the public merge promise resolves.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One selected ref and one repository per explicit merge invocation; repository size affects Git merge/status/refs costs, but the diff does not increase their cardinality.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One merge subprocess at a time for this invocation. Repository-lock retries are sequential and pre-existing; post-merge state queries use the existing bounded Promise.all fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: VS Code configuration is read from the extension-host configuration service on each explicit merge; there is no new external cache or miss path. Git and model-refresh cache behavior is unchanged.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: all callers converge on Repository.merge, the setting defaults false, and the generated arguments remain exactly `git merge <ref>` on this path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Repository-dependent merge and refresh durations vary, but the changed disabled-setting path adds only a local configuration lookup and no expensive boundary or extra multiplicity.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the common/default path preserves subprocess count, arguments, concurrency, and refresh work.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: The local configuration lookup selects `-S`; the existing Git merge subprocess then creates and cryptographically signs one merge commit before the existing model refresh runs. Signing is required behavior for this opt-in setting.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run the existing `git merge` process with the added `-S` argument.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One Git process per explicit merge invocation, as before.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One `git merge <ref>` process ran, but it did not honor the enabled VS Code signing setting.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The process is awaited before refresh and command completion.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Git invokes the configured GPG, X.509, or SSH signing backend to sign the newly created merge commit.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one signing operation for the one merge commit; no signing occurs when the merge creates no commit.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: VS Code's merge command omitted `-S`, so this opt-in signing work did not occur unless Git's own configuration independently enabled it.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cryptographic signing and any signing-agent interaction are necessarily on the merge-commit creation path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run the existing repository model refresh after the merge.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One bounded refresh per merge result.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same refresh already occurred after an unsigned merge.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One signature for the single merge commit produced by one explicit merge invocation; it does not scale with files, commits being merged, refs, or repositories beyond separate user-issued merges.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The merge and its Git-managed signing helper are serial on the command critical path. No Promise.all or per-item loop creates concurrent signing; repository-lock retries remain sequential.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The setting is resolved per repository at invocation time. Signing-agent/key caching is owned by the configured Git signing backend and unchanged by this code; no application cache is introduced or defeated.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed argument directly requests one Git signature only when the resource-scoped setting is true, and merge operations are not collection-driven or concurrent.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Signing latency depends on backend, agent state, hardware token, and prompts, but cardinality is strictly one and the work is the explicit semantics of the enabled setting.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable performance regression: the single additional signing boundary is intentional, opt-in, bounded, and inseparable from the requested signed-merge behavior.

Scenarios.Scenario: Fast-forward or conflicting merge with git.enableCommitSigning enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The existing `git merge -S <ref>` process runs. Fast-forward merges create no commit and therefore do not invoke signing; conflicting merges stop before commit creation and are later concluded through the existing commit flow. The existing model refresh remains awaited.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run `git merge -S <ref>` without creating a merge commit on fast-forward or conflict.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same one Git merge subprocess ran without `-S`; neither form invokes a signing helper when no commit is created.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must determine fast-forward success or conflicts before refresh/UI progress can complete.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Execute the pre-existing post-operation repository refresh, including status/refs and merge-state checks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One bounded refresh for this operation.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One selected ref per explicit operation; conflict count and repository size affect pre-existing Git/status work, but the diff adds no per-conflict or per-file work.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One merge subprocess, followed by the existing bounded refresh. Any later conflict-resolution commit is a separate serialized user action using the pre-existing commit path.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No new cache is involved. The resource-scoped configuration lookup is local and signing-agent caches are not touched when no merge commit is created.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: `-S` requests signing of a commit only if Git creates one, while the diff contains no loops, retained state, or scheduling changes.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Git's merge and refresh durations depend on repository size and conflict volume, but no new signing operation occurs in these no-commit cases.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: subprocess count and expensive work remain effectively unchanged for merge attempts that create no merge commit.

Analysis.Summary: Reviewed all three changed files and all merge entry points. The diff adds one resource-scoped in-process configuration read and conditionally requests a single Git-managed signature for an opted-in merge commit. It introduces no collection fan-out, repeated refresh, concurrency burst, cache-lifecycle issue, or unbounded retention; default, fast-forward, and conflict paths preserve existing expensive-boundary cardinality.
